FROM OUR STATE EXCHANGES.
A knitting factory, with a capital of $25,000, is to be established at Madison.

A petition is in circulation for the removal of the land office from Menasha to Oconto.

The aggregate loss by the Durand fire is stated to be $50,000 and the insurance $10,000.

Arrangements are being made for starting a paper mill with a capital of $25,000 at Eau Claire.

Over 1,000 names were secured to the pledge during the recent temperance revival in Whitewater.

A young man, named Leonard, was killed by a falling tree in Emmet Horan's lumber camp on the Eau Claire, on the 20th.

The loss by the burning of Kickbusch's sash and blind factory, at Wausau, recently, was $15,000. The insurance was but $2,000.

Simon Ottoson was robbed of a gold watch and a sum of money by two highwaymen in Racine a night or two ago. No clue to the robbers.

Considerable attention is being given to the improvement of sheep in some portions of Sheboygan county, especially in the vicinity of Hingham.

Green Bay Gazette: A gentleman from Marquette informs the reporter of the Gazette that the weather in that region reminded one of spring; clear water was seen over the lake and several tugs were plying between different points.

MR. WM. GRENZOW, of Spring Grove, had $46 stolen out of a bureau drawer in his house while he was attending church in this village last Sunday. The preacher was right in saying that members should bring their pocket books to church.

SPARTA HEBALD: Mr. Simeon S. Snattuck, living northwest of town, was presented with a broken leg for Christmas. Sunday morning he attempted jumping across a small stream, alighting on his right foot, and falling backward on the left, breaking the leg below the knee.

FOND DU LAC Commonwealth: A rumor reaches this city that Charles LaFour, who is well-known in police circles here, killed a man at Superior City, Lake Superior, and was lynched by a mob. An effort was made to-day to get the truth in the matter, but nothing certain has yet been learned.

STEVENS POINT Gazette: The Green Bay, Stevens Point and Northern R. R. has entered the city and rails have been laid as far as Owen Clark's lumber office. We are now connected with an iron band on this route with Green Bay on the east and Winona, Minn., on the west, giving us railroad facilities second to no city in this section of the state, and still the day is not far distant until we will have another road and perhaps two.

EAU CLAIRE News: John Powell, aged 83, a resident of the town of Brunswick, was drowned on Saturday last in a small lake near his residence. It seems the old gentleman went out on the ice to fish and venturing out too near the open water the ice gave way and he fell in. No one being present, he was unable to get out and soon drowned. As he did not return at the usual time his son went out in search of him and was soon horror-struck at finding the place where he broke through. Procuring assistance, the body was rescued. The funeral took place on Monday.

GREEN BAY Daily Data: A sad case of desertion is that related by Mrs. Rika Klein, who has been in this part of the state for the past two weeks in search of her husband Henry Klein, alias Henry Wolf, who has abandoned her to abscond with a woman to whom he had been engaged before marrying his present wife. The injured wife traced the pair to Menasha, but there lost track of them. She learned, however, that they had been married, without Henry's having gone through the formality of procuring a divorce. Mrs. Klein is very anxious to discover the whereabouts of Klein, as she and her children are left in strait-ened circumstances. The injured wife has given up the search, and left last evening over the Northwestern road for her home in Milwaukee.

EAU CLAIRE Free Fress, December 24th: We were informed on Friday evening, by Mr. William Ebner, just arrived in this city, that on the morning of the 20th inst. a barn and shed owned by the Knapp, Stout & Co. company, at Twenty-two-mile Ford, 22 miles north of Menomonie, were burned to the ground, entailing a loss estimated at $4,000; that the entire contents, comprising six horses, six mules, harnesses, two carriages, reapers, mowers and other farm machinery, and 1,500 bushels of oats, burned with the buildings; that a belief prevailed that the fire was the work of an incendiary, as the fumes of kerosene were noticed around the burning premises while the fire was raging; that the clearing out of the ruins is going on now, and that the company will rebuild the destroyed structures immediately.

A Horse Thief Lynched.
SON. June 27th — The followin
TUCSON, June 27th. The following has been received from Fort Thomas: Deputy Sheriff G. A. Stevens and District-Attorney Bolon started from here yesterday morning with a noted Mexican horse thief named Epifance, as prisoner. When about two miles from Smithville they were stopped by about thirty masked men, who took the prisoner and hanged him. The lynchers are supposed to be Mormons. The prisoner had just returned from Tucson, where he had been in the hospital, under treatment for a gunshot wound in the head. The citizens generally commend the act, and hope it will serve as a warning to others.

GLEANED FROM THE MORNING MAILS.

The Incidents and Accidents of Daily Life—Tragic Occurrences and Events of Current Interest.

There was a $50,000 fire at St, Mary's, N. B., last evening.

The schooner George A. Hunt, valued at $16,000, was burned at her dock in New York yesterday.

James Joyce, a Brooklyn, N. Y., milkman, committed suicide on Monday night by shooting himself in the mouth.

The winning horses at Coney Island yesterday were Hilarity, Colonel Sprague, Woodflower, Eole, Blenheim and Kitty Clark.

Emory & Johnson's furniture factory and other adjacent property at Portland, N. B., were burned last night. Loss, $20,000.

The Chinese merchants of San Francisco have telegraphed $300 to Governor Kirkwood for the sufferers by the late cyclone.

A boiler in the Jackson fire clay company's building, Jackson, Mich., exploded instantly killing Michael Nugent and seriously injuring six others.

Charles Roberts, aged 15, son of the locktender, fell into the canal at Northumberland yesterday afternoon and was drowned. It is supposed that he was seized with a falling fit.

George Phuidt, aged 14 years died at New York on Monday night of lockjaw, the result of a pistol shot wound in the left hand inflicted by himself on the 16th instant.

The first new wheat from Virginia was sold on 'Change at Baltimore yesterday, for $1.80 and $1.65 per bushel. Of two small lots the first was good but the other was quite damp.

Advices from Stanley, Falkland Islands, state that the British ship Star of Brunswick, from Huanillos April 26 for the United Kingdom, has stranded at Bullport and will probably be a wreck. Five of the crew were drowned.

Foster, alias Armandale, charged with shooting with intent to kill the Munroe boy and girl at East Dalhousie, Annapolis county, N. S., last winter, yesterday, at Halifax, pleaded guilty to shooting the boy and not to shooting the girl. He was sentenced to the penitentiary for life.

The opening sale of the Sprague estates under a trust mortgage was made in Providence yesterday. Four parcels of real estate on Dorrance, Friendship, Pine and Orange streets, Providence, were sold by auction at from $1.60 to $40 per foot. All were purchased by the Union company.

James Milliken, who had been in Egypt for four years, returned to Hollidaysburg a few days ago. Upon seeing him his wife became insane. Believing that he would never return, she had obtained an absolute divorce but a short time before. The unfortunate lady, it is thought, will have to be taken to an asylum.

Lynched by Mormons.

A dispatch left from Ft. Thomas says that officers left there with a noted Mexican horse thief named Epiffance in custody. Two miles from Smithville a band of masked men took the prisoner and hanged him. The lynchers are supposed to be Mormons.

Result of a Drunken Ralld.

A true bill was found by the Pittsburgh grand jury against Jury Commissioner Sands, who, in connection with three Fifth ward roughs, raided a Chinese laundry and stole a sum of money from the proprietor. He, together with the others, was held in $1,000 bail for trial at court.

How Mayor Stubbs Was Killed.

A young man named Delaire was arrested at Polk City, Iowa, on suspicion of being the murderer of R. P. Stubbs, the mayor of that city, last April. Under threat of lynching, Delaire confessed that a gang numbering fifteen had plotted to rob Stubbs, and he brought desperadoes from Missouri named Wickes and Blackman to do the work and that Wickes did the killing. The same party robbed the bank in Kansas City some time since. Delaire's sister was working at Stubbs' and knew of money in the house.

A Duke Nearly Drowned.

The Duke of Edinburgh, while fishing recently near Bayona, Spain, hooked a large fish. In his attempts to haul it in he lost his footing and was dragged into water sixteen feet deep. He was carried under four times. After struggling for half an hour he succeeded in reaching land.

Carry the News to Cooper.

The burgess elected last spring in Media, Delaware county, having declined to serve on account of a legal technicality, an election to fill the vacancy was held. Stalwart and Independent lines were drawn on the issue and Henry Green, a rabid Stewart Independent, was elected over William Campbell, Stalwart, formerly prison inspector. It was a clear cut Independent success in Cooper's own borough and shows which way the wind blows.

The Debris Matter Again-The Recent Marine Disasters.
SAN FRANCISCO, June 27.—A circular, signed by A. C. Bingham, Mayor of Marysville, and C. E. Sexey, President of the Sacramento Valley Anti-Debris Association, has been sent to the Hydraulic Mining Companies, demanding, under the recent decision, that after fifteen days no more debris be run into the rivers on pain of prosecution.

The bark Roswell Sprague, which took fire, yesterday, soon after passing to sea and towed back here and beached, will prove a total loss. The vessel is valued at $20,000. The cargo is valued at $15,000. Insurance unknown.

The Consular inquiry into the loss of the steamer Escambia has completed its findings, which are that the disaster was owing to the slowing down of the engines without the Captain's orders while crossing the bar, causing the ship to fall into a trough and allowing seas to board her. The Court does not think the vessel lacked stability, though on that point the evidence is somewhat conflicting. The evidence shows the ship was properly loaded. The Captain was exculpated. Loss of the ship due to the perils of the sea.

Tucson, June 27.—The Sonora Railroad will be completed to Magdalena in about five weeks. Last week an incendiary fired one of the railroad buildings in Hermosillo, destroying $30,000 worth of material. The criminal was arrested and under the laws of the State will probably be shot. Magdalena is being fast Americanized. A dozen saloons are opened and a distillery established. Americans are opening business. Hermosillo is growing rigidly. Ice works and a sash and blind factory will be completed in two weeks. Water works have been constructed by the city. A State University is being built. Guaymas, also, is erecting water works. Shipping interests are active. Several new shipping agencies have been recently opened. A line from Hermosillo to Paso Del Norte has been determined on. It will be about 400 miles.

Belligerent Tape Measurers.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 27.—A small war took place on Sansome street this morning. The Bell Telephone Company wished to put up a pole on the side in front of Murphy, Grant & Co.'s building. The firm objected and kept special police on duty all night to prevent work. The police left at daybreak, and the telephone men at once made a descent and planted a pole, which penetrated the basement of the building. On the arrival of the employes of the firm, the counter junrpers made an attack in force. Black eyes and bloody noses resulted. The telephone men were routed and the pole thrown down. A number of clerks were arrested and bailed out by the firm.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 27.—A Fort Thomas, Arizona, dispatch says: Officers left here yesterday with the noted Mexican horse-thief, Epifance, in custody. Two miles from Smithville a band of masked men took the prisoner and hanged him. The lynchers are supposed to be Mormons.

Suicide of a Pioneer.

AUBURN (Cal.), June 27.—George H. Stevens committed suicide last night by taking morphine. The deceased was a pioneer; but lately business reverses and extravagant habits rendered him penniless. He has lately been in Arizona.

Another Marine Disaster.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 27.—A telegram to the Merchants' Exchange says: The British ship Lammermoor, Captain Duncan, from Sydney, for San Francisco, went ashore on Bodega Reef. Probably a total loss. There are seven feet of water in the hold. Rolling heavily. The crew was saved by a schooner.

Severe Earthquake.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 27.—A sharp earthquake occurred at half-past 5 o'clock this morning. No damage reported.

Another Warrior Seeking Justice.

WASHINGTON, June 28.—The secretary of war has under consideration the case of Major-General G. K. Warren, now lieutenant-colonel of engineers, who was relieved from command of the fifth corps at the battle of Five Forks, Va., in 1865 by General Sheridan. Warren made several efforts to have the matter investigated, but without avail until 1879, when President Hayes appointed a committee of inquiry, Major-General Hancock as president. The committee completed their report a few months ago; and a record of the case was submitted to Judge Advocate General Swaim for review. The committee found that General Sheridan had not exceeded his authority, but that in one or two instances he had misjudged the conduct of General Warren. The judge advocate general is said to approve the general finding of the court. It is not a case requiring further action. The record in the case comprises over seven thousand pages of foolscap, the largest that ever passed through the bureau of military justice.

Big Springs.
Special to the Herald.
Big Springs, March 27.—About ten days since six negro convicts escaped from a gang working for the Texas & Pacific out west, killing one guard. They robbed a camp on the Texas & Pacific, and secured arms, rations, and civilians' clothing. Two made their way safely to Mexico, and the other four traveled east along the road, pursued by Captain McMurray's rangers. They broke into several section-houses for rations. Saturday the sergeant came upon them lying in the brush near the roadway and ordered them to hold up their hands. They ran off, and two were killed and the other two captured.

The eminent gentleman in spectacles goes to work in cold blood to make everybody miserable by proving to his own satisfaction that in seventeen millions of years this globe will be only an iceberg from the Pole to the Equator, and the sun, but a huge red ball, having, like the Prodigal Son, squandered all its caloric substance, and only fit to feed on husks among the celestial swine, so to speak. In a recent divorce case in a New York court one of the lawyers, in the course of a flowery oration, stated that the reason why Osman Pasha exposed himself so recklessly in battle during the war of three years ago was that he had seven wives. This was going a long way for a simile, and it is safe to presume that cynical statement came from a bachelor. The inuendo is that excessive matrimony drives men to desperation and makes them regardless of life—willing to meet the ills they know not of rather than endure those they have. Of all reasoning this is the most absurd. The man who is called to fight for his altars and his fires puts in his work in proportion to the number of altars and fires he has to fight for and not as one seeking death to escape his domestic responsibilities. The Murdered Deputy Collector.
DETAILS OF THE KILLING OF JAMES M. DAVIS BY MOONSHINERS IN TENNESSEE.

Deputy Collector James M. Davis, of the internal revenue service, who was waylaid and murdered by moonshiners near Nashville, Tenn., a few days ago, was one of the most valuable men in the service. The commissioner of internal revenue says he never hesitated to do his duty, no matter what the odds, and that he was as brave as a lion. He has long been a terror to moonshiners, and they have been trying hard to get him out of the way. About a year ago he had his hip broken and his skull fractured in two places. Commissioner Raum ordered him here at once, and he was under the care of Dr. Bliss for some time. He entirely recovered from his injuries, and since has done good work. His assassination is quite a blow to the internal revenue service. Although Commissioner Raum is anxious to bring the assassins to justice, it is generally believed in Tennessee that the reward of $300 for each is insufficient to secure their arrest, as all are regarded as desperate men, well used to handling firearms.

A gentleman, who arrived at Nashville from the mountains a few days ago, said that if Davis had had half a chance he would singly and alone have fought his assassins, eight to twelve in number; was riding without a saddle girth, which had been lost, so that when the horse jumped at the first fire he was thrown to the ground. He lay on the earth as if dead for a short time, having been hit in the leg. He finally got up and started back limping, when the bushwhackers began to fire at him and he again fell prostrate. One of the assassins then walked up upon the embankment and shot the top of his head off with a double-barrelled shotgun. Davis and his prisoner. Vickers, were allowed to pass the ambuscade before the murderers fired upon him. It was thought that this was done in order to get Vickers out of range of their shots. Davis, wounded as he was, fired three shots, while U. S. Commissioner Campbell, who was 150 yards behind, fired one shot. After they had killed Davis the party departed, taking a path leading over Ben Lomond Mountain, above McMinnville, whence they came. They were seen in the suburbs of McMinnville on the morning preceding the assassination and some persons talking to them. One hundred shots were fired. Twenty-six bullet holes were found in the back portion of Davis' coat.

Capt. Jas. M. Davis Killed.
Deputy Collector Davis and his men were returning from Beersheba Springs to this place Monday last, and when about three miles from here Davis was fired upon by some parties in ambush. At the first fire Thomas Vickers, who was riding with Davis, fled. When shot Davis fell from his horse, but soon regained his feet and started back up the road toward Campbell and Cathcart who were in the rear. He had not gone far, however, when he was fired upon again and killed. An inquest was held and the body was brought to town. Between twenty and thirty bullets were found in the body and the skull was litterally shattered with pistol balls.

The shooting was done by men concealed behind breastworks constructed of logs and cord-wood and covered over with cedar brush. This structure was about ten feet from the Beersheba road and the underbrush had been cut away so as to leave an unobstructed view. The assaulting party is estimated at from 10 to 15 men, George Campbell, who has been with Davis a long time, and was with him on this trip, states that Davis' conduct was very strange for two or three days prior to his death, that he manifested signs of restlessness and depression altogether unusual in him. Vickers states that Davis was laughing and telling a long anecdote when he rode into the deadly ambush and the shooting began.

DAVIS' DEATH.
A Presentiment Which Made Him Restive.
It appears that Davis had a presentiment that he would be killed before he got off the mountains. In consequence he was restive from the time he left McMinnville. When he had reached a point not far from the ambuseade on the Beersheba road, Vickers says Davis called his attention to some loose horses on Ben Lomond mountain, but Vickers could not observe them. Davis had been to Beersheba and was on his way to McMinnville. His assassins had come over the point at Ben Lomond mountain. At one place on the mountain the road to the rear could be observed for a distance of two miles. When Davis and his men came in sight, on this part of the road, a pistol shot was fired. This was believed to have been a signal to the assassins that Davis and his men had come in sight, and for them to make all the necessary arrangements to kill him. The shooting did not occur until half an hour after the signal. Before reaching the ambuseade Davis got Vickers to get down and let out his stirrup straps, that he might simply touch the stirrups with his toes. The ambush was so constructed that each one of the eight men had a porthole through which he could fire, the base of it being a large log, with wings, made of cord wood, thrown out in front and on each side, and covered with cedar. It is believed the oysters, in the cans found, must have been eaten on some day previous to the assassination. It is said that in their testimony before the coroner's jury, two wood-choppers within fifteen feet of whom the assassins passed, denied having known the men. The white man testified that he thought he knew five of the men when they were approaching him, but he was satisfied he did not know any of them after they had passed by him. The negro testified that he did not know any of the men in the crowd and could not identify any one of them. They came upon him and his white companion so unexpectedly that he was scared and said to them out of fear, perhaps, more than anything else, "we surrender," supposing they had come after them, but why he could not tell. None of the men said anything, and went off in another direction.

It is thought that the two wood choppers, even if they had recognized any of the men, would not dare to say so from fear of the vengeance of the assassins or their friends. It will thus be very difficult to discover the men who killed Davis.

Some men are suspected of having taken part in the assassination, but it is doubtless whether the real assassins will ever be found.—[American.

The Richmond State of the 29th contains an account of the killing of a negro in Moore county by a member of a sheriff's posse. The details are as follows. The homicide took place in the county, jail, where the prisoner, Willis Edwards, a stout negro man about twenty-five years of age, was confined on a peace warrant. He became desperate because the sheriff informed him that he would have to remain in jail until court time. He raved and swore in an outrageous manner, tore planks from the ceiling with his bare hands and told the sheriff that if he could get at him he would kill him. The sheriff reported to a magistrate that Edwards was desperate and would soon break out of jail. The magistrate told him to take the prisoner out of the cell and chain him in the dungeon till he became quiet. A posse were summoned for that purpose and its members were increased as the desperate disposition of the man became more apparent. In the meantime a large crowd had gathered in the corridors of the jail. Edwards denied the crowd, cursing them, said he would kill the first man that laid hands upon him, that he would kill somebody if he ever got out, anyway, and told the sheriff he might as well get his rope ready to hang him. An attempt was made to take him, when he rushed into the corridors, swinging a piece of plank right and left among the crowd, but in the struggle he finally got into the cell again, carrying Mr. Berry Birford with him. He struck the gentleman two on three severe blows with the piece of scantling, and was preparing to strike him again when Mr. Binford shot him twice in the back, and right arm, upon which he fell. Willis also broke the fingers of a Mr. Robert Simpson in the affray. The negro lived one hour after the shooting, and a post-mortem examination showed that one ball passed through the kidneys, the second through the liver, and the fourth shattered the bone in the right arm. It is thought this shot was fired by some other party, as the ball was smaller than those from Mr. Binford's pistol, which were of a thirty-two calibre. The coroner's jury rendered a verdict that the negro Willis Edwards came to his death by pistol shots fired by B. H. Binford in self-defence, and that the shooting was justifiable. Mr. Binford's injuries were quite severe. He suffered from two severe blows, one on the neck, and the other on the shoulder. The blow delivered on the neck was a slanting one, otherwise it would have killed him instantly.

Shot in Jail and Dies of His Wounds.
Just at the close of the last term of our Superior Court, Wilson Edwards, colored, of Sandy Ridge Township, was lodged in jail, for want of bondsmen, a peace warrant having been sworn out against him by a colored woman whom he had endeavored to shoot.

On Wednesday, when his dinner was sent up, he was found lying on the floor of his cell, without coat or shirt on, and sullenly refused to take his dinner. In an hour afterward, Sheriff Price went up and found him still lying on the floor, in a sullen mood, and in reply to the question as to why he didn't eat his dinner, used profane and abusive language. From this and other matters, Sheriff Price thought perhaps his mind was wrong, and that he had better be ironed before hurting himself or some one else. He sent off and procured the help of three or four stout colored men, but upon their arrival he was found to be in the notion of fighting, and threatened to kill any one who entered the cell; and being well armed with heavy stuff torn from the ceiling of his cell, he was rightly considered a dangerous customer. By this time, other help came, among them several white men—J. E. W. Austin, Jno. S. Richardson, B. H. Binford, E. T. wade, Rob't Simpson, and others—and as it was dangerous to go into the room where he was, he having all advantages, it was decided that it was best to open the door and allow him to come out, and overpower him, as he came. But it was found that he was harder to manage than they had anticipated, and he came so quick, with a stick in each hand, and his naked body so slick he could not be held, that he took the crowd somewhat by surprise, and began striking right and left with his murderous weapons. Ben. Blakeney, colored, was the first victim, he having been punched in the mouth with a stick, before the door was opened. Rob't Simpson next had two fingers broken. Berry H. Binford was next struck about the neck, and from this the negro's spite seemed to centre on Binford, and he followed him on across the passage into an opposite dungeon, where he "got in" another blow, which brought Mr. B. to the wall. Just here, three shots were fired, and though they entered the negro's body and two of them produced fatal wounds, he struggled on until forced to the floor by J. Richardson, who had swung to a handkerchief the negro had around his neck. After he was down, it was known that he was seriously hurt, and physicians were sent for, and Dr. Welsh soon came and said there was no chance to save him. In the meantime, Mr. Binford was taken to a room below and Dr. Ramsay called in, who found his patient badly hurt and suffering greatly from the blow on the side of the neck and shoulder. Had this blow been otherwise than a glancing one, Binford would, in all probability, have been instantly killed.

The negro died in less than an hour—one ball having passed through the liver, a second just above, while a third went through the kidney.

Afterwards, a former fellow-prisoner who was taken from the cell only a few days ago, told Sheriff Price that the prisoner, Edwards, had disclosed to him a plan he had formed to escape, which was to "play off crazy," and should Sheriff A. J. Price come alone and open the door he would brain him and rush out. Should the Sheriff come with help he would fight his way through and escape or be killed in the attempt. He was a powerful, well muscled, able-bodied negro 30 or 35 years old, and was known as a desperate character. The affair of course is to be greatly regretted but no blame can be attached to any one, as it was necessary to iron him if possible or he would have torn up the jail and come out, and after the effort was made it became necessary to fire on him or he would have killed others.

Since Edwards had been jailed, conclusive evidence has been brought out, showing that he was the person who shot Jack Huneycutt, col'd, some time ago, in Sandy Ridge Township, mention of which was made in this paper at the time.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict that the killing was in self-defense and justifiable.—Monroe Enquirer.

Frankfort-on-the-Main, containing a population of about 100,000, is said to be the richest city of its size in the world. If its wealth were equally divided among the inhabitants, every man, woman and child would have, it is said, some $4,000 apiece. There are, as may be supposed, many poor people in the town; but the citizens are, as a whole, in unusually comfortable circumstances—more so, probably, than the citizens of any other capital in Germany or Europe. It is stated that there are 100 Frankforters worth from $4,000,000 to $7,000,000 each, and 250 who are worth $3,000,000 and upward. The city is one of the great banking centres of the globe. Its aggregate banking capital is estimated at $2,000,000,000, more than one-fourth of which the famous Rothschilds—whose original and parent house is there—own and control. The annual transactions in bills of exchange are in excess of $100,000,000.

A TEST FOR INSANITY.—Dr. Lamson will not have died in vain if the suggestion made by one of the British authorities on insanity is hereafter applied to test the perceptive faculties of alleged insane murderers. The suggestion is that a red hot poker be handed to the said alleged insane person; if he takes it, he is to be adjudged as really unable to distinguish between right and wrong; but if he refuses it, then he is to he considered as responsible and be made to suffer accordingly. The test is a very simple one, and there seems to be no reason why it should not be accepted as satisfactory. He who can remember that a red hot poker burns can also remember to kill another is a crime.—London Graphic.

The opening of the Western North Carolina Railroad from Asheville to Warm Springs, and the quick connection arrangements with the Tennessee railroads, are beginning to effect a revolution in travel east and west. Pullman sleepers are put on at Greensboro. At Henry passengers going west get breakfast, and then take seats in an observation car, from whence they get views of the grand scenery all the way from Henry's to Warm Springs.

He was so expert that the Mayor and Marshal forbid his giving public exhibitions of lock picking.

THE Universal Peace Union convened in Washington on the 28th.

EIGHT prisoners, including two murderers and one highway robber, effected their escape from the jail at Tuscaloosa, Ala., on the 27th, by cutting the hinges off the cell door and running over the jailer.

THE Governor of Michigan has ordered an investigation into the truth of affidavits charging N. Delong, Mayor of Muskegon, with attempting to bribe an Alderman to vote for one of his nominees to office.

A. F. BRACKMAN, who for some weeks was the laughing-stock of St. Louis, died the other day in the Missouri Insane Asylum. He came from Nebraska with an abundance of money, married a chambermaid at the Planters' House, gave her a wardrobe costing $1,500, and was deserted on the day succeeding the wedding. He was several times arrested for eccentric conduct on the streets. An autopsy revealed the fact that he died from softening of the brain.

WILLIAM A. HALL, the thieving Assistant Auditor of Newark, N. J., has been captured at Toronto. He spent three months at Prescott, where he kept two fast horses and carried a large amount in diamonds. He is said to have secured $40,000 in plunder.
JOHN C. WOLCOTT, the best-known lawyer in Western Massachusetts, has been jailed in Boston to make him sober. Then he will be arraigned in the federal court for charging a pensioner $100 for prosecuting his claim.

BRAVE BEAR, the Sioux Indian who would have been executed on the 9th of March for the murder of a soldier named Johnson, near Fort Sully, Dak., but for an appeal to the Supreme Court and motion for a new trial, has been resentenced to be hanged on the 20th of July, the Supreme Court having denied him a trial. He fully deserves the sentence, as he is clearly guilty not only of this murder, but of others, including an entire white family near Pembina. Upon being asked if he had anything to say before being sentenced, Brave Bear replied: "I have taken the white man's part always. I am disappointed at the treatment of the white man. They can do as they please with me, and cut me to pieces if they choose." So saying he received the sentence with the utmost unconcern.

At Springfield, Ohio, May 29, a man named Kitzmiller, becoming enraged at his daughter for keeping company with a man of whom he disapproved, drew a revolver and shot her dead. He narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of his neighbors before he was taken to jail.

MARCUS DE BASTIDE, a young French Canadian, was assaulted by members of the congregation of the French Canadian Catholic chapel in New York City, May 28. The cause of the assault was the distribution by Bastide of tracts printed in French calculated to persuade people to accept Protestant beliefs. He had attended services at the chapel and the officiating clergyman denounced his books to the congregation.

A COLLISION between trackmen of the Denver & New Orleans and Denver & Rio Grande roads occurred near Denver, Colo., May 28. The latter road undertook to block the progress of the former by running an empty engine under a full head of steam into a gang of men laying the track at a crossing. None of the men were injured, but the engine was derailed and plowed up the track for a considerable distance.

WILLIS EDWARDS, a notorious desperado, was killed in the jail at Monroe Court-house, N. C., the other day, in an affray with the Sheriff and his posse. Edwards succeeded in severely wounding the four men who attempted to subdue him.

FRANK MILLER, while robbing the residence of H. P. Moore at Erie, Pa., the other night, was nearly beheaded with a scythe.

The Attorney-General has decided that Secretary Kirkwood is not eligible for appointment on the Tariff Commission.

F. H. STONER and Arthur J. Cole, of Chicago, were drowned, May 27, by the cap-sizing of a boat.

Kansas City, April 3.—The news of the killing of Jesse James created an immense sensation in this city, although the report was generally treated with discredit and even at this late hour many unbelievers can be found. This afternoon as soon as the news was received here Police Commissioner Craig left for St. Joseph with a heavily armed posse of men to guard the body of James and furnish protection for the man who killed him. At the station house it was learned that a young man who has been hanging about the station for several weeks past, was the person who shot and killed Jesse James. Ford left this city about a week since and joined James in the vicinity of St. Joseph, remaining with him until an opportunity to kill him was found. From the police it is learned that Ford, who is said to be a member of the gang, was under control of Craig, and has been used as an instrument for James' destruction. Omaha, Neb., April 3.—The report is telegraphed from Sioux City that the Union Pacific had determined to abandon all work on the Oregon Short Line is without any foundation whatever. Assistant General Manager Kemball, of the Union Pacific, says that every nerve is being strained to push the Oregon Short Line as rapidly as possible. The track has been laid within eight miles of Snake river, Montana. The bridge across Snake river will be in position in a few weeks, and a large grading force will soon commence work on the west side of the Snake river and from there to Wood river and Boise City, Idaho, work will be rapidly rushed forward. Steel rails have been contracted for and are being rooled and shipped to the front. It is expected this season to grade to Boise City and to lay between three and four hundred miles of track. Nashville, Tenn., April 3.—An American's Murfreesboro special says: O'Brien, a special deputy sheriff, went out last night to arrest Bethel Thompson, who shot an officer in Shelbyville last year when about to be arrested for horse stealing. An exchange threatens his delinquent subscribers after this fashion:

Now we have got 'em. Some news paper publisher has found the following law made expressly for those who refuse to pay for their paper; so it will be necessary for that class of subscribers to come to time hereafter. It says: "A new postal law or decision authorizes the publishers of newspapers to arrest any man as a thief who takes his paper and refuses to pay for. This is a fair and a judicious law, and should have been enacted years ago, as means of protection to publishers, for there are lots of persons who will take a paper for a time, and when asked to pay for it will laugh at the publishers, and tauntingly defy him to get it if he can. In this manner ublishers lose hundreds of dollars. The law is intended to meet just such rascals, and publishers generally should unite in having it enforced.

The reaper and mower trade is dull in Richmond, for the reason that our dealers have sold out all the stock they had on hand. The demand was large.

The brick work on Jo. Sanderson's new business house is progressing finely, and if the workmen could have suitable weather, it would soon be finished.

Harvesters are making things rattle this week between showers. If we could only have a week of settled weather the wheat would all be nicely cut and shocked and some of it stacked.

Rev. Dr. Flack, of Excelsior, was in the city on Friday night last. He is a very pleasant gentleman and by his energy and zeal has built up a considerable town at Excelsior.

Mr. Jas. A. Tuttle has sold his saddle and harness shop in this city to Mr. Hudgins, who will continue the business at the old stand on west side of the square. If he advertises his business well he will make money.

Uncle Billy Griffey was in town yesterday and called in. He says he thinks of running for State Senator on the U. T. P. tickets, and proposes to give the boys a lively hustle. He wants the DEMOCRAT to draw it mild on him, and of course we will.

Dr. J. D. Taylor and family, who left here some months ago, to make their home in Chillicothe, we learn will return at once and locate permanently in Richmond again. After all they find there is no place like home. We gladly welcome them to our midst once more.

Mr. Thomas Holt has sold his interest in the store of Holt & Woodson, under this office, to his partner, Harry Woodson, who will conduct the business in the future at the old stand. He will keep a full stock at all times and do you right. Don't forget the place.

We are in reciept of a copy of a little pamphlet entitled "Ingersoll Unmasked," by Clark Braden, of New York. If he give a correct account of the early life of Ingersoll, he ought to have been confined in a house of correction when young and subjected to severe treatment, as he certainly was a bad boy and soon developed into a drunken bad man, and age has not improved him.

Prof. B. F. Duncan, who has occupied the responsible position of President of Richmond College in this city for three years, has been elected to the position of principal of the public schools at Gallatin, Daviess county. While we regret very much losing Prof. Duncan from Richmond, we rejoice that he is called to so pleasant a town as Gallatin. He is a worthy gentleman an earnest christian, a good citizen and one among the best educationalists that has ever dwelt among us, and he will reflect honor on any community in which he may dwell. The good people of Gallatin can rest assured that they have drawn a prize, in securing the services of Prof. Duncan, and they should give him that earnest support necessary to make his work complete. He has the best wishes of the editor of this paper for his future success and prosperity.

We are astonished that our well informed neighbor Col. Child should fall into the error of accepting a little, cheap electioneering clap trap, gotten off during our recent primary, for fact. In order to scare a few men, one of the tickets was call a whisky ticket, but did it have any advantage oper the other in this respect. Let us see. The short ticket or one supposed to have been the Temperance, had on it the name of one saloon keeper, and had the positive suppors of three out of four saloons in town kept by Democrats, Col. Child certainly was not aware of these facts when he fell into the error of saying that the question of Temperance cut any figure in the contest. It is true, we are proud to say, that the ticket, all the way through, is composed of sober men and men whom no Temperance man could refuse to support on that ground, but the scallawag who runs the Excelsior Herald, will not lose an opportunity to throw dirt at them if he gets an opportunity. Mark that prediction.

"The lips which touch liquor shall never touch mine," is a good motto for young women to adopt, and having once adopted it stick to it. We would say to a young lady, contemplating matrimony, never marry a man if he gets drunk. Better get into your coffin, pull the lid down and be buried alive than to marry a man who gets drunk, as your torture will be less and you will be the quicker out of your misery. There are now in this world too many broken, crushed, disheatened wives with poor, pithless, worthless, drunken husbands who make of home a hell. Too many weak, worn, wicked, worthless wrecks who love liquor for the opportunity that it give them to get away on drunks, associate with other loafers, dirty their garments and wallow in the gutter. If you do not wish to get into a coffin, tie a piece of stinking meat in your bosom so you will always have it there to smell of and to rub up against you, and you will be as happy and contented as you ever can be with a droozling, slobbering mumbling, grumbling, incoherent, gutter-seeking wretch of humanity for a husband, or rather for a dead-weight or disgrace—that is if you are sensitive in your nature.
